## Chosen hook

Line 1 (Investigator, aimed at what a test was designed to find, never at whoever ordered it):

"A normal full blood count does not rule out an iron problem. It was never built to."

Re-hook: "Your stores run down before your blood count moves, and that gap is where most missed iron in men sits."

## Script

**Funnel:** MOFU (Capture) | job: myth-bust plus mechanism (iron deficiency without anaemia) | cta: canonical-article | format: linkedin-post | marker: ferritin
**Emotion:** Surprise resolving into recognition. The man who checked and was told he was fine gets a reason that is not "you imagined it".
**Source:** `ferritin-blood-test` (Pillar D hub, published 2026-06-22, Ewa-signed).

POST

> A normal full blood count does not rule out an iron problem. It was never built to.
>
> Your stores run down before your blood count moves, and that gap is where most missed iron in men sits.
>
> Ferritin is the protein your body stores iron in. It measures the reserve, the tank, rather than the fuel currently in the line. The tank empties first. A full blood count is built to catch anaemia, which is what happens further down that road, so your ferritin can be low while your blood count still reads perfectly normal.
>
> That has a name. Iron deficiency without anaemia. It is the commonest version of low iron that gets missed.
>
> There is a second gap, and it sits inside the range rather than outside it. In the UK, ferritin under 30 points to depleted stores. But a man can sit at 35, see "normal" printed on his report, and still feel flat, because that range was built to flag anaemia rather than to tell you where your energy and recovery sit best. Normal for the lab and optimal for you are two different questions.
>
> The reason this gets missed in men specifically is that most of us were told it is not our problem. Iron is filed under something other people have to think about. So it is checked last, if at all.
>
> Now the part I will not soften, because the article it comes from does not soften it either. A low iron result in a man is a GP conversation, not a supplement order. Iron carries a real overdose risk, and depleted stores in a man can be the first sign of something that needs finding rather than topping up. Measuring tells you where you stand. It does not tell you why, and the why belongs with your GP.
>
> That is the whole reason I am building Andro Prime the way I am. We will tell you what your number is and hand you the context. We will not sell you the thing your result seems to point at.
>
> If you have ever been told your bloods were normal, do you know which test that was, and what it was actually looking for?

**First comment:** I am building Andro Prime, plain-English men's health read from your blood. The full version, with the UK bands, what a single reading cannot tell you, and the four points where this belongs with your GP rather than with us, is here: https://andro-prime.com/blog/ferritin-blood-test?utm_source=linkedin

## Craft notes

- **Structure chosen on avatar fit, and that is the axis it was ranked on.** The competing angle was the tank-versus-tap explainer, which is the hub's own opening device and reads well. It was rejected because its implicit ask is "learn this mechanism", which is more reading for a man whose problem is already an excess of unassessed reading (`avatar-mark.md` §A). The chosen angle asks him to reinterpret a result he has already been given and already accepted, in one pass. It also lands directly on a verbatim Tier 2 pain point: "I never even thought to check iron because I'm a guy and everything I read said men don't get iron deficient." Both angles clear compliance identically and neither carries a first-hand result, so they sit on the same proof rung (`hook-rubric.md` §4) and avatar fit was the only live axis.
- **Archetype:** Investigator, which `hook-playbook.md` §2 names as one of our two natural homes. The contrast is "you think that test answered this question; it was built to answer a different one". The energy is aimed at what an instrument was designed to detect, never at the person who ordered it, which is the line §2 draws.
- **Device 7, understatement at the peak:** "That has a name. Iron deficiency without anaemia." Two short sentences carrying the turn, adjectives cut rather than added.
- **The GP rail is carried, not dropped.** A derivative may not add a claim, and it should not quietly shed its source's safety line either. The hub's firmest paragraph is that a low result in a man goes to a GP rather than to a supplement, and it survives here almost intact, including the two reasons. Dropping it would make the derivative softer than the asset it inherits from, which is the same failure as exceeding it, pointed the other way.
- **The two figures are UK reference bands quoted from the hub (NICE CKS), not personal results.** 30 is the UK deficiency cut-off; 35 is the hub's own worked example of a technically-normal reading. No bloodwork of Keith's appears, and nothing is written as Mark.
- **Distance from the other Kit 2 assets.** `four-worth-seeing` argued which markers were worth running. `four-things-on-the-sheet` argued how to read a printout. This one argues that a test you already passed was answering a different question, which is a claim about instrument design rather than about coverage or literacy. `c-07` in the queue is the ferritin short and uses the tank-not-the-tap device, so the two do not collide.
- **`cta: canonical-article`, deviating from the queue row.** `content-queue.md` L-06 says `kit-2`. The post links once, to the hub, and the hub carries its own Kit 2 routing onward. Tagging the second hop would overstate direct kit routing in any report built off this field, which is exactly the case `canonical-article` was added for on 2026-07-31 (Observation 88). It also keeps a MOFU asset off a direct kit CTA, per `content-funnel-map.md`.
